title: AI’s Zero Payoff: Apollo Economist Says Most Companies Won’t Profit from Current AI Investments
body:
The promise that artificial‑intelligence tools would soon become a profit engine for every Fortune‑500 firm has not materialised, according to a new note from the chief economist at Apollo Global Management. The analysis, which surveyed spending patterns and earnings reports across a broad swath of corporate America, concluded that AI initiatives have generated essentially “zero financial payoff” for companies outside the technology sector, despite billions of dollars poured into software licences, talent and pilot projects over the past two years.

The economist’s findings stem from a deep‑dive into public filings, investor presentations and internal data from more than 200 non‑tech firms spanning manufacturing, retail, energy and financial services. While many of these organisations have launched high‑profile AI pilots—ranging from predictive maintenance in heavy‑industry plants to chat‑bot customer service in retail chains—their balance sheets show no discernible uplift in revenue, margin or cash flow that can be directly attributed to the new technologies. In contrast, pure‑play software and cloud providers have reported double‑digit growth tied to AI‑related products, underscoring a stark sectoral divide.

Several factors appear to be dampening AI’s impact on the broader corporate landscape. First, the integration challenge remains formidable: legacy IT systems, fragmented data silos and entrenched processes often require extensive re‑engineering before AI models can be deployed at scale. Companies that have invested in off‑the‑shelf generative tools, for instance, frequently encounter “pilot fatigue” as pilots stall in the proof‑of‑concept stage without moving into production. Second, the talent shortage has forced many firms to rely on external consultants or short‑term contracts, inflating costs while limiting the development of in‑house expertise needed for continuous model refinement. Finally, the hype cycle has led to premature adoption, with executives chasing headline‑grabbing AI use‑cases rather than aligning projects with clear, measurable business outcomes.

The report also highlights a disparity in how AI spending is accounted for. Many corporations treat AI expenditures as operating expenses, which are expensed immediately, rather than capitalising them as long‑term assets. This accounting treatment obscures any potential future benefits and makes it harder for investors to assess the true return on investment. Moreover, the lack of standardised metrics for AI performance means that success is often gauged qualitatively—through internal dashboards or anecdotal improvements—rather than through hard financial indicators such as incremental earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation (EBITDA).

Despite the sobering conclusions, the economist cautions against dismissing AI outright. He points to a handful of outliers—primarily in the logistics and pharmaceutical sectors—where targeted AI applications have begun to shave costs or accelerate product development cycles. These cases suggest that the technology’s value proposition may be highly contingent on industry‑specific dynamics, data quality, and the willingness of senior leadership to commit to long‑term transformation rather than quick‑win experiments.

Looking ahead, the analysis implies that the next wave of AI investment will need to be more disciplined. Companies are likely to shift focus from broad, speculative deployments to narrowly defined projects with clear ROI metrics, tighter integration with existing systems, and robust governance frameworks to manage data privacy and model bias. As the market matures, investors may also demand greater transparency on AI spend and its contribution to earnings, prompting firms to adopt more rigorous reporting standards. In this environment, the firms that can successfully bridge the gap between cutting‑edge algorithms and tangible operational improvements stand to be the true beneficiaries of the AI revolution, while the rest may continue to see the technology remain a costly experiment rather than a profit driver.
